deep.reconstruction:
Heading: 'Functionen mit verschiedenen Periodicitätsmoduln' (functions with different moduli of periodicity); the word 'Periodicität' is written above the line as an insertion. Riemann takes a doubly periodic function f with periods (Periodicitätsmoduln) k1 and k2. Then every m k1 + n k2 with m, n integers is also a period: f(z + m k1 + n k2) = f(z). These periods form the period lattice Λ = Z k1 + Z k2.

He then introduces new moduli l1 = α k1 + β k2 and l2 = γ k1 + δ k2 with αδ − βγ = 1. Integrality of α, β, γ, δ is implicit; supplying it is my addition. He concludes: 'Die Periodicität bleibt dieselbe, wenn statt k1 und k2 aufgefaßt werden l1 und l2 als Moduln der Periodicität', i.e. the periodicity is unchanged if l1, l2 are taken as the moduli instead of k1, k2.

Implicit justification (mine): l1 and l2 are integer combinations of k1 and k2, so they lie in Λ. Because the determinant is 1, the inverse is k1 = δ l1 − β l2 and k2 = −γ l1 + α l2, again with integer coefficients. Hence Z l1 + Z l2 = Z k1 + Z k2.

This is the standard change of basis of a period lattice by a matrix in SL2(Z), the starting point of the theory of the modular transformation of elliptic functions. The crossed-out marginal words ('Doppelte Periodicität') show he first labelled the topic as double periodicity. The page is unrelated to the PDE computation on the previous page (a hyperbolic equation in u and log ρ) and to the next page (retarded potential f(r − αt)/r).
errors: No mathematical error. Integrality of α, β, γ, δ is not stated but is needed. Determinant −1 would also preserve the lattice (with orientation reversed); taking +1 is the conventional choice that keeps the orientation (sign of Im(k2/k1)).

results.what: Two bases (k1, k2) and (l1, l2) = (αk1 + βk2, γk1 + δk2) with integer coefficients and αδ − βγ = 1 generate the same period lattice, so they describe the same double periodicity.
results.modern_name: Change of basis of a lattice / SL2(Z) action on period pairs (modular transformation)
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi and Abel (1820s–1830s, transformation theory of elliptic functions); systematized by Eisenstein, Weierstrass and Hermite.

deep.surprise_reason: Elementary and well-known fact. Riemann used period lattices and their bases throughout his work on elliptic and Abelian functions, so a brief note of this is entirely expected.

checkable.sympy: a,b,c,d,k1,k2=symbols('a b c d k1 k2'); M=Matrix([[a,b],[c,d]]); simplify(M.inv().subs(d,(1+b*c)/a) - Matrix([[(1+b*c)/a,-b],[-c,a]]))
checkable.asserts: When ad − bc = 1, the inverse matrix is [[d, −b], [−c, a]], which has integer entries if a, b, c, d are integers; so k1, k2 are integer combinations of l1, l2.

checkable.sympy: a,b,c,d,k1,k2=symbols('a b c d k1 k2'); l1=a*k1+b*k2; l2=c*k1+d*k2; expand(d*l1-b*l2 - (a*d-b*c)*k1)
checkable.asserts: d*l1 − b*l2 = (ad − bc)*k1, which equals k1 when ad − bc = 1 (result simplifies to 0).

checkable.sympy: a,b,c,d,k1,k2=symbols('a b c d k1 k2'); l1=a*k1+b*k2; l2=c*k1+d*k2; expand(-c*l1+a*l2 - (a*d-b*c)*k2)
checkable.asserts: −c*l1 + a*l2 = (ad − bc)*k2, which equals k2 when ad − bc = 1 (result simplifies to 0).

transcription_corrections: The left-hand side of the first equation is l1 (written so it resembles k1 with an accent), not k1'. The text below refers to 'l1 und l2'.
First line: the crossed-out 'Periodicitätsmoduln' is followed by 'k1, k2' (or 'k1 + k2'). The '[?]' symbols after it are an illegible marginal mark, not mathematics.
'mk1 + nk2' has the letters m and n overwritten/corrected but reads as an integer combination of the periods.
The crossed-out marginal words are 'Doppelte Periodicität' (both struck).
